speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Almost half of the world's population have gone or will go to the polls this year.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Research conducted by London-based technology company, SumSub, suggests that the numbers are alarming.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the deepfake video you just watched did not convince you of its impersonation of me, more advanced versions soon will.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Around the world, countries have recognised the need to mitigate the harms of deepfakes to their elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To date, 388 deepfakes have been taken down by the National Election Commission of South Korea during its elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another example is Brazil, which has banned synthetic electoral propaganda that will harm or favour any candidate during an election.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The sanctions include the revocation of the candidate's registration or their mandate if they had been elected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Australian government is also considering the advice of its Electoral Commission to regulate the use of AI in elections, given the Commission's recent warning that it has limited scope to protect voters from deepfake videos and phone calls imitating politicians in Australia's upcoming elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not just governments which are concerned.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The technology industry has also recognised the dangers of electoral deepfakes and the importance of ensuring voters can exercise their choice, free from AI-based manipulation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Twenty leading tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and TikTok, signed the Tech Accord at the Munich Security Conference in February, committing to combat the deceptive use of AI in elections this year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the face of these developments, Singaporeans are rightly concerned.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One study shows that more than six in 10 Singaporeans are worried about the potential impact of deepfakes on the next election.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In a 2021 ruling on a case related to misinformation and online falsehoods, our apex Court had said, "It is simply incompatible with the core principles of democracy to procure the outcome of an election to public office or a referendum by trading in disinformation and falsehoods." Mr Speaker, I hope Members will agree that AI-generated misinformation can seriously threaten our democratic foundations and demands an equally serious response.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The ELIONA Bill will amend our election laws to prohibit the publication of content that: (a) is or includes Online Election Advertising (OEA); (b) is digitally generated or manipulated; and (c) depicts a candidate saying or doing something that he or she did not, in fact, say or do; (d) but is realistic enough that some members of the public who see or hear the content would reasonably believe that the candidate did, in fact, say or do that thing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will go through each of these criteria in detail.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, OEA under our existing elections laws refers to any information or material published online that can reasonably be regarded as intended to promote or procure or prejudice the electoral success or prospects of a candidate or political party.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The existing OEA provisions guide the transparent and responsible use of the Internet during elections, including for campaigning; and ensure that the elections are contested fairly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The ELIONA Bill strengthens OEA regime by targeting the substantive content of OEA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, the ELIONA Bill is scoped to address content that is digitally generated or manipulated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This includes content generated or manipulated using AI techniques, such as generative AI.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It also includes non-AI techniques, such as Photoshop, dubbing and splicing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are now seen as more traditional editing methods, but they can still be used to manipulate content depicting candidates, making them as harmful and misleading as AI-generated deepfakes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, the ELIONA Bill is scoped to address the most harmful types of content in the context of elections, which is content that misleads or deceives the public about a candidate through a false representation of his speech or actions that is realistic enough to be reasonably believed by some members of the public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The condition of being realistic will be objectively assessed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is no one-size-fits-all set of criteria but some general points can be made.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, such content should closely match the candidates' known features, expressions and mannerisms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Technically, we would expect a degree of sophistication resulting in minimal inconsistencies in aspects like lighting, body movements or audio distortions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, content may make use of actual persons, events and places so that the false representation appears more believable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, a fake rally speech touching on current affairs looks more real when placed against the backdrop of an actual and familiar rally site.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We must also recognise that audiences perceive and process the same content through different lenses shaped by their individual experiences, beliefs and cognitive biases.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, many of us find it incredible that the Prime Minister would be giving investment advice on social media.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But as Members of Parliament, we have all met residents who have fallen prey to such AI-enabled scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will elaborate on this later in my speech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It does not matter if the content is favourable or unfavourable to any candidate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As we propose this new measure to tackle realistic misrepresentations of candidates online, we are mindful not to disallow reasonable use of AI or technology in electoral campaigning.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While each case will be assessed on a case-by-case basis, there are several scenarios that the prohibition will not extend to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first is AI-generated or animated characters and cartoons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most of these animations are not photorealistic replicas of real persons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Audiences will generally be able to tell that the speech or actions depicted are not real.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second is benign cosmetic alterations, such as the use of beauty filters or colour and lighting adjustments of images and videos.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such alterations typically involve modifications that do not materially affect truthfulness and do not result in a misrepresentation of a candidate's speech or actions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The third is entertainment content, such as memes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We recognise that such content can arise as part of online discourse during the election period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Memes will not be caught under the law as long as they are assessed to be unrealistic and do not mislead audiences about a candidate's speech or actions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some Members may be concerned, will candidates' regular campaign posters, showing individuals against the backdrop of a group representation constituency (GRC) or a single member constituency (SMC), be prohibited if they are put online?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such posters are usually obvious composite images, such as candidates disproportionately superimposed in front of a landmark or backdrop.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members of the public would not reasonably believe such content to be realistic depictions of a candidate's action.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such campaign posters are unlikely to fall within the scope of prohibitions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, the Bill does not extend to private or domestic communications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This refers to content shared between individuals or within a closed group, like group chats with family or a small group of friends, in view of user privacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That said, we know that false content can circulate rapidly on open WhatsApp or Telegram channels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If it is reported that prohibited content is being communicated in big group chats that involve many users who are strangers to one another and are freely accessible by the public, such communications will be caught under the Bill and we will assess if action should be taken.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The factors that determine whether communications are private or domestic are set out in the respective election Acts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, the prohibition does not apply to news published by authorised news agencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is to give space to fair reporting on prohibited content, such that the public can be alerted to the false content about candidates in a timely manner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, we recognise that a layperson may carelessly reshare messages and links without realising that the content has been manipulated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The legislation provides for a defence if a person did not know and had no reason to believe that the candidate did not, in fact, say or do the thing and inadvertently commits the offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, pay the election deposit; and second, consent for their names to be made public by the Elections Department (ELD).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The consent form will be made available via the ELD website.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The intent is for the website to be updated daily.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Paying the election deposit is a prerequisite for standing in an election and an indicator of an individual's seriousness of intent to be a candidate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a step up from simply making a public declaration of one's potential candidacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Publishing the names of those who placed the deposit will also make clear to the public which individuals are covered by the law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is the candidate's choice entirely when to inform the public about his or her intention to stand for election before Nomination Day.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Candidates can choose to put down the election deposit but withhold consent to make their names public until Nomination Day.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, individuals themselves should also readily come forward to clarify and debunk content that they believe misrepresents them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government will use a range of detection tools to assess if the content has been generated or manipulated using digital means.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have at our disposal commercial tools and also those developed in-house or in partnership with researchers, such as those at the Centre of Advanced Technologies in Online Safety, or CATOS.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These tools are constantly updated to keep up with technology.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In reviewing reports of false content flagged under this new prohibition, the Government will prioritise candidates' reports to the Returning Officer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides the technical assessment on whether the content has been manipulated, the Returning Officer will also rely on candidates' declarations on whether the content falsely depicts their speech and actions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have placed significant weight on candidates' declarations to the Returning Officer under this new prohibition, as the candidate is in the best position to speedily clarify if the content is a truthful and accurate representation of himself or herself.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government is unlikely to have all the evidence of whether a candidate actually said or did something, especially if it was in a private setting.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The declaration by candidates will be made to the Returning Officer, for candidates to attest to the veracity of his or her claim.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This declaration form will be made available to candidates via the Candidates' Portal on ELD's website.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The penalties for an illegal practice are set out in the elections Acts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If convicted of an illegal practice, one may face a fine not exceeding $2,000 and become ineligible to be elected as a Member of Parliament (MP) or the President.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Further, if already elected, the election of a candidate as a MP or President may also be invalidated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Currently, the Returning Officer has powers to issue corrective directions to any relevant person, including social media services, to remove or disable access in Singapore to prohibited OEA, or to stop or reduce its electronic communication activity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The ELIONA Bill extends these powers for the Returning Officer to issue corrective directions against this new category of content and corrective actions must be taken within the specified period of time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As mentioned earlier, the Government will prioritise candidates' reports and declarations to the Returning Officer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If assessed to be a genuine case, the Returning Officer will issue corrective directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Only in exceptional cases will directions be considered against false representations without a candidate's declaration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This may arise when the objective facts are widely known or if the Government has access to data that reliably confirms the candidate's actual speech or action.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The public can also report potentially prohibited content of candidates to the authorities for review.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To better equip the public to make informed choices during the elections, the public will be notified about corrective directions that have been issued against offending content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Non-compliance with a corrective direction issued by the Returning Officer is an offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The revised penalty is on par with similar offences under other content regulation tools like the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA), the Broadcasting Act (BA) and the Online Criminal Harms Act (OCHA).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For all others, including individuals, there is no change to the financial and custodial penalties for non-compliance with a corrective direction and remains at a fine not exceeding $1,000, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or to both.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have engaged major social media services on the requirements under the ELIONA Bill and shared our expectation that such directions are to be promptly complied with to uphold the integrity of our elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, the Bill addresses the most harmful digitally generated and manipulated content, including deepfakes, that can influence electoral outcomes, while recognising the value of novel content creation techniques and the desire of candidates to employ innovative methods to engage voters.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, the safeguards apply to all candidates, regardless of political party and potential impact of the fake content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This recognises that fake content favourable to one candidate must be unfavourable to another and vice versa.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our voters must be able to make informed choices based on factual and truthful representation of our prospective political leaders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Candidates, too, have a responsibility to conduct themselves with integrity during the elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The ELIONA Bill updates our suite of measures introduced over the years to address various forms of harmful online content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During and outside the election periods, existing content regulation tools will continue to apply to certain types of AI-generated misinformation and deepfakes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, under POFMA, a Minister, or an appointed Alternate Authority during the election periods, may issue a direction for a recipient to communicate a correction notice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under OCHA, directions may be given to deal with online activities that are criminal in nature, such as deepfake-related scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under the Protection from Harassment Act, individuals may seek recourse for certain content that have caused personal harassment, alarm or distress to the individual.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Beyond the expectations set out in the ELIONA Bill during the election period, social media services should also bear greater responsibility for digitally generated or manipulated content at all times.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This includes an obligation to put in place adequate systems and processes to enhance the transparency of digitally generated or manipulated content, such as through labelling.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I believe that many people have experienced friends or family members around us believing in deepfakes online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: No matter how we try to explain to them, they still believe in the fake content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Sometimes, even we can be deceived, and the spread of fake content is very difficult to guard against.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), deepfakes will only become more prevalent and realistic, allowing individuals with ulterior motives to sow seeds of doubt in our society more easily and quickly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If such fake content is widely disseminated during a General Election, the consequences could be too dire to imagine.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Enhancing the public's ability to discern the authenticity of content is the most effective preventive measure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, let us work together to be more vigilant about online content, and verify them against reliable sources when necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Everyone should do their part and be the first line of defence against fake content. : Sir, the ELIONA Bill will add an additional layer of safeguards to our elections, but everyone – candidates, citizens, tech platforms – has a part to play in protecting our democracy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We must keep our elections fair and honest, conducted on the basis of fact, not fiction.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By and large, Members of this House, regardless of party allegiance, have supported these ideals and I appeal to Members to stand behind this Bill so that we can continue to uphold the integrity of our elections.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a response to the increasingly sophisticated technological threats we face today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I believe that robust legislation requires careful consideration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also needs clear articulation to avoid unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this spirit, I seek several clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must carefully maintain the balance between two critical elements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are our citizens' fundamental right to freedom of expression and our collective responsibility to share information responsibly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill introduces significant penalties for sharing digitally altered content.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Instead, supporters or proxies, including fake accounts, generate these messages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Deepfake videos and misinformation can circulate not just on social media, but also through messaging channels, such as WhatsApp and Telegram.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are transmitted very quickly and can go viral easily.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These channels are, hence, often more damaging than we realise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Specifically, how will it deal with deepfakes or messages shared through these supposedly private communication channels?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While we acknowledge the need to balance freedom of expression, we must also differentiate between harmless satire and intentional falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This distinction applies even if the content is shared privately.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must remember – private does not mean harmless.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, we need to address concerns regarding political overreach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The vagueness of certain definitions within the Bill could be concerning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The terms "realistic but false representations" and "manipulated content" are broad.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I understand the need to capture the evolving nature of digital manipulation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, this breadth could lead to confusion or inconsistent application.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It could even lead to potential overreach in enforcement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Ministry to offer greater clarity on this point.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, how does the Ministry intend to differentiate between malicious manipulation and minor alterations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would include artistic edits or satirical content.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They ensure that this law meets its purpose while avoiding the stifling of legitimate political expression.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry provide examples of content that would fall under this Bill's purview?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must confront concerns about potential selective enforcement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The enforcement mechanisms could be seen as vulnerable to bias.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is particularly true for the provision allowing corrective directions by the Returning Officer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such bias could lead to possible allegations of selective application.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What concrete assurances can the Ministry provide to guarantee transparency and impartiality?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the enforcement of this Bill remain demonstrably free from any unfair allegations of political bias?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is critical, especially since the Bill empowers candidates to request such corrective directions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is essential to balance efficiency and due process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that fake accounts and deepfakes are not just detected but swiftly taken down before they poison public opinion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, I wonder if we are being harsh enough.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should we, for instance, mandate that perpetrators bear the onus of ensuring complete removal of such content from the Internet rather than simply issuing a correction notice?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many would simply ignore a correction notice and continue consuming the content.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should we not implement more punitive measures by working with social media companies to take down fake content?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Considering the large amount of resources potentially incurred for rectifying the damage, we should consider holding perpetrators accountable for it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must acknowledge the challenges posed by rapid technological advancements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this Bill focuses on identifying and mitigating manipulated content, we must recognise that detection technology may lag behind AI-driven content generation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Harmful content could spread before effective action can be taken.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given the fast-evolving nature of AI and digital manipulation, how does the Ministry plan to stay ahead?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What systems, partnerships or research initiatives will ensure robust detection capabilities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will corrective actions be taken swiftly and accurately?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mr Speaker, Sir, legislative measures must be coupled with public awareness and education.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our citizens deserve the power to discern truth from lies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They must protect themselves and our democracy from the invisible hand of manipulation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not enough to penalise the creators of misinformation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must arm our citizens with the tools to fight it themselves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to equip them to critically assess digital media, identify manipulation and avoid falling prey to misinformation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It requires a sustained, long-term investment in digital literacy programmes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond penalties, is the Ministry planning any public education campaigns?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Specifically, are there initiatives addressing AI-generated misinformation and improving digital literacy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will these efforts be tailored to different demographics?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sixth, Mr Speaker, Sir, this Bill needs further clarification regarding its application to foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While it prohibits election advertising by foreign entities, the borderless nature of online content makes preventing foreign interference a challenge.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Ministry plan to address cases where content from overseas is designed to influence our elections?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What protocols are in place to track, identify and block foreign-sourced digital manipulation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can this be enforced on foreign-based entities, for instance, online media outlets based in foreign jurisdictions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must consider whether the timeframe for this Bill's provisions is sufficient.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could we establish a "pre-election period" with safeguards to address early content?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The rapid spread of online content demands an equally rapid response.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is critical for protecting the integrity of our election process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Globally, we have seen the threat that deepfakes pose to elections.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, in Moldova, a video of the President endorsing a pro-Russian political party caused public discord; in Slovakia, audio clips surfaced of a liberal party leader allegedly discussing vote rigging; and in the US, AI-generated content showed a dystopian future following President Biden's re-election bid.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The threat of deepfakes is not a distant possibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Deepfakes of our Senior Minister and Prime Minister have been used to promote fake investment products.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We saw just now a deepfake of Minister Josephine Teo.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This highlights the potential for misuse, even outside election cycles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These examples show that the threat is real, immediate and happening globally.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Deepfakes can erode trust, destroy reputations and mislead citizens.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot allow technology to hijack our democracy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is why I have raised several key questions today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Free speech should not be a free pass for spreading falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill must carefully balance the freedom of speech with measures to counter misinformation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It needs clear definitions and safeguards against biased enforcement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, how will this Bill tackle fake accounts and deepfakes from private messaging channels?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must invest in sophisticated technology to stay agile in the face of AI advancements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is equally important to empower citizens with digital literacy skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Addressing foreign interference and ensuring swift enforcement within the election timeline is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Democracy must be defended not just at the ballot box, but in the digital space.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us create legislation that safeguards our democracy and elections while protecting our citizens.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While exciting, technological advances in the field of generative AI bring new challenges in maintaining the integrity of our political and electoral system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The proliferation of highly realistic yet fabricated content, particularly in the digital realm, poses a risk to our electoral system and, if we are not careful, will shake the trust citizens have in the democratic process here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It bears reiterating that deepfakes and digitally altered content are a very real and present danger to democracy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As mentioned by the Minister and also Member Yip Hon Weng earlier, in the 2023 Slovak parliamentary elections, we witnessed the potential impact on elections of the malicious use of deepfakes to sway the results of an election.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just two days before the elections there, during the equivalent of our cooling-off day, a fake audio clip surfaced, which was set to have been a recording of pro-European candidate, Michal Simecka, discussing electoral fraud with a prominent journalist.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Both quickly denied its authenticity but the clip went viral.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The impact was also amplified by the deepfake being released during the election's "silence period", when media is prohibited from discussing election-related developments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In that election, the pro-Russia candidate Robert Fico ultimately won, which naturally led to speculation about whether the deepfake contributed towards Simecka's loss, given that he was polling stronger than the ultimate victor.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While political scientists on the whole concluded that the deepfake alone did not cost Simecka to lose, the very speculation caused by its going viral laid bare how dangerous it is for a democracy to exist in an environment of low trust in public institutions and a population with a propensity to believe in conspiracy theories.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the new section 42L(4) contains a number of carve-outs from the band of manipulated content during the election period for OEA, including for authorised news agencies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The reason given for this is to allow factual reporting.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, this is not enough reason to exempt these actors as factual reporting should not require reproduction of prohibited material.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, we should consider a concerning scenario – authorised news agencies, when reporting on prohibited content, might inadvertently spread misinformation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In our attention deficit world, many readers skim headlines and images without carefully reading the full article or captions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This creates a risk where such content, even when presented as part of factual reporting, could be mistaken for genuine content and go viral as real news.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, the very act of reporting by reproducing these prohibited materials might unintentionally amplify their reach and impact.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our disquiet over creating such a two-tier media landscape leads to questions about how we can ensure that media entities exempt from the prohibitions of the Act do not publish such content without consequences.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More specifically, does the Minister believe that the existing codes of practice governing authorised news agencies are sufficient to address the concerns raised above, or would further updates be needed to combat the unique risks associated with digitally manipulated content and deepfakes?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, the Bill also states that private or domestic communications are exempted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The new section 61M(4) exempts private or domestic electronic communications between two or more individuals from the regulations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we acknowledge the intent to protect personal privacy, we hope that this exemption does not become a Trojan horse used to overcome the Bill's defences combating disinformation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is because disinformation often spreads rapidly through private channels.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also not a secret that modern communication platforms have blurred the lines between private and public spaces.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What would be the standing of spaces such as private Facebook groups, private Telegram channels, locked Facebook profiles or messaging group chats?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would whether a channel is private hinge on whether having people in the group not knowing each other, for example?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is important to have clarity on this as academics have found that there is emerging evidence that propagandists increasingly exploit applications such as WhatsApp and Telegram, preying on their popularity, loose moderation policies and trust within private networks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In Slovakia, the example I raised earlier, Telegram has become a haven for pro-Russian propaganda and a deepfake of Simecka was spread widely on Pro-Fico Telegram channels ahead of the election.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, can the Minister clarify how the exemption for private messages will address the risks associated with widespread disinformation spreading through these channels?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Aside from these, I have some clarifications around three broad areas: first, the scoping of the prohibitions; second, questions about the reporting and investigation of alleged offences; and third, the potential misuse of the regime.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On the scoping of the prohibitions, I note that the prohibitions and offences only apply during election periods and it is confined to Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Deceptive information may begin swaying public opinion well before an election is formally announced and this is especially the case as the potential window for calling a general election narrows over time.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, foreign disinformation groups are known to wage persistent year-round disinformation campaigns to influence political outcomes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, the government of Canada detected a Chinese spamouflage campaign, where various Canadian members of parliament, including its' prime minister, leader of the opposition and members of the cabinet were targeted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The rapid response mechanism alerted the affected members of parliament who were provided with advice and support on how to protect themselves from the campaign.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To discredit and denigrate targeted members of parliament, by questioning the political and ethical standards, using deepfake videos and fake social media profiles.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the punishments outlined in this Bill are meant to act as strong deterrence, they do not fully address threats from those operating outside of Singapore's jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How then will we effectively combat the risks associated with a foreign coordinated campaign using prohibited content like deepfakes?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, moving to an investigation of alleged offences.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that members of the public can report alleged prohibited content, where and what is the investigative capacity to investigate claims made in this regard?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Who undertakes the investigation, and how long would it take for these to be completed, before any further action is taken?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What resources, both in terms of manpower and otherwise, would be available to the Returning Officer and ELD to make relevant decisions and take enforcement action?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, in Singapore, we are somewhat unique in having a very short campaign period and added together with the quick spread of digital information, it makes it even more imperative that decisions about claims have to be made rapidly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also, what happens after an offence is reported and the decision is made to issue a corrective order?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the Returning Officer then simultaneously ask both the poster and platform to take it down?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What then happens if there is a refusal to comply with the order?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the Minister also be able to elaborate on any appeals process, if one were to disagree with the corrective order?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is particularly important too, as information has now gotten to the stage where experts sometimes even disagree about whether a piece of content is real or doctored.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we often view deepfakes as malignant and harmful, recent elections such as the recently concluded Indian national elections have seen instances where generative AI and deepfake technology has been used to manipulate videos of candidates in a way to benefit them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A classic example would be using deepfake technology to show candidates speaking in languages or dialects that they do not themselves speak, in a misleading effort to endear themselves to certain segments of the electorate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And how will this be communicated so that members of the public do not spam reports as an act of mischief during the election campaign?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In a 2020 paper, Orben warns against what he terms as "technology panics", arguing that these can sometimes encourage quick fixes that "centralise control over truth".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe that Member Mr Yip also raised similar concerns about overreach earlier.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, I think it would be more helpful to invest in nuanced and effective proactive public education strategies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A technique that appears promising is "pre-bunking", the process of debunking lies, tactics or sources before they strike, because prevention is more impactful than cure.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It works like inoculation and aims to build mental resilience against misinformation before being exposed to its full force.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Much like Ministry of Defence's Exercise SG Ready earlier this year involving a simulated phishing exercise run by organisations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Pre-bunking works by exposing people to weakened forms of misinformation and uses this to teach them to spot manipulative techniques used by fake news peddlers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This approach seems to work across different cultures and across those with differing political views and should be integrated into our wider strategy tackling the effects of misinformation on our population.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we stand at the intersection of rapid technological advancements and evolving societal dynamics, it is crucial that our legal framework keeps pace with the changes in the world – in terms of changing technology, information dissemination and diverse electorate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Countries around the world have begun taking legislative steps to combat the potential misuse of deepfake technology, particularly in electoral context.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The US, for example, has seen various states introduce Bills aimed at regulating deepfakes, especially during election periods.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some states have enacted laws that prohibit the use of deepfakes to deceive voters, particularly close to elections.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, the federal government has started considering regulations focused on transparency and accountability in political advertising.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Meanwhile, the United Kingdom (UK) has been exploring the implications of deepfakes on democracy, suggesting that existing laws on misinformation need to be updated to specifically address deepfakes, with a focus on protecting electoral integrity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Deepfake technology poses a significant threat to our democracy and electoral process by creating realistic but false content that can mislead voters, distort public opinion and undermine confidence in the validity of elections.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through audio and video manipulation, deepfakes can be weaponised to spread misinformation, damage reputations and sow confusion during critical moments in elections.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The speed at which manipulated content can spread on social media only increases the risk of potentially influencing a large portion of voters before the information's authenticity can be verified.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This erosion of trust is dangerous as it weakens the foundations of a fair and transparent electoral system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Everyone should be concerned and vigilant about this threat because it has the power to distort truth in ways that are difficult to detect and refute.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In an electoral context, this could mean voters making decisions based on falsehoods or maliciously wrong content.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Singaporeans and concerned members of the public, we must be cautious about the information that we receive and share, especially in the digital space.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Critical thinking, media literacy and verifying the authenticity of content before sharing are key responsibilities that we should all shoulder in facing this ever-growing threat.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To protect against the dangers of deepfakes, the Government, technology companies and individuals need to work together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Legislative measures are in place to address false content during elections and ensure that those behind such malicious actions and intentions are held accountable.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Social media platforms must enhance their ability to detect false or misleading content.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, public awareness campaigns can help educate citizens on how to recognise manipulated media content.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through vigilance, legal protections and responsible content sharing, we can safeguard our democratic system from treacherous elements seeking to mislead and divide our people through technologies like deepfakes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, these developments reflect a growing international recognition of the dangers deepfakes pose to electoral processes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Transparency, accountability and public awareness are the cornerstones of these legislative efforts and our Bill today is part of this global movement to safeguard the integrity of elections.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This clarification is welcome as I believe that the Bill itself does not define the election period and it is somewhat unclear in the Parliamentary Elections Act which only defines the postal voting period.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the clear and certain timeline that the Bill seeks to address, which is within the election period only.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should avoid chilling free expressions of speech outside of election periods.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I thank the hon Minister for her assurance just now during the Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second clarification is on the disclaimers for AI-generated content and satire.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill rightly offers some defences for those accused of spreading deepfake content.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This means that a person forwarding a link by an authorised news agency to his family members in a WhatsApp group chat might not be considered an offence, if that person did not know or had no reason to believe that the representation of the election candidate was false.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, we should still emphasise for the need for the public to be responsible and, as far as possible, ascertain the truth and veracity of the source of the information before spreading such information.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be in line with our vision of building a nation of discerning digital natives who are vigilant to guard against online falsehoods and disinformation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, we must also consider content that is obviously labelled as generated by AI or created for satire purposes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would such labelling be sufficient to avoid any liability on the part of the content creator, even if such content was done by AI or deepfake, and is clearly meant not to be relied upon for the truth of its contents?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The downside is that, due to the brief but intense period of election, the harm that such contents would do may outweigh the considerations for artistic licences, as not many people may have the time or context to understand that the content is satire.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A case in point is the Australian case involving the deepfake video of a Queensland premier, Annastacia Palaszczuk, in 2020.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The post depicted the premier as hosting a press conference claiming that the state was "in massive debt" and had "huge unemployment".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The deepfake video then had her as saying "I would like your vote on 31 October, but if you want to get rid of us, I completely understand." She obviously did not say any of this and this is entirely not true.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In California, the law on deepfakes makes an exception for satire or parody, provided that such content is labelled as such.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The defamation laws only provide full defences for fair comment, justification and privilege.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, there are clear elements to establish the tort of defamation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And lastly, there must be a reference to the complainant.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Singapore Court of Appeal has held that defamation also includes inferences or implications that the ordinary, reasonable person may draw from those words in the light of general knowledge, commonsense and experience.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, if the content is premised on an untruth or deepfake, then they should be caught by this offence even if there is a clear disclaimer because the cost of social media clicks and comedy cannot come at the price of our politics and democracy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the sensitive nature of election periods, content creators should be mindful of their responsibilities to ensure that their work is not based on untruths or deepfake.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would encourage more responsibility content creation and dissemination.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My third and last set of clarifications is on the due process and procedure.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An important aspect of this Bill is the due process afforded to individuals or entities accused of distributing deepfake content.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Returning Officer has the power to issue corrective directions and candidates can request such directions under the new section 61MA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we must ensure that the process is not open to abuse.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the hon Minister's clarification that there will be a requisite form for such reporting and penalties for abuse of the same.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the seriousness and severity of the consequences, perhaps it is important that any such request for a corrective direction be accompanied by a statutory declaration and, if necessary, a Police report, to demonstrate the seriousness of the claim.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There must also be safeguards to prevent the law from being abused as a political tool to take down legitimate election content.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This also provides a basis for recourse for a business or someone who is not a candidate but was nevertheless adversely impacted or affected by such false content to possibly seek consequential damages after the election period.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must also ensure that the content in question is truly a deepfake before any corrective action is taken.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the rapid advances in technology, it has become increasingly difficult to detect deepfake.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While early signs, such as unsynchronised lips or unnatural lighting, could previously indicate a deepfake, generative AI technology has now reached a level that is beyond where these signs are no longer reliable.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This underscores the need for the Government to allocate sufficient resources to keep pace with these advancements.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another critical issue is the potential misuse of deepfake technology to create false endorsements from non-candidates, such as influencers or public figures.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, in the heat of campaigning for the US presidential elections, global superstar Taylor Swift was recently the target of fake images implying her endorsement of a particular political candidate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This prompted her to publicly endorse another candidate to prevent future falsehoods from happening again.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such instances highlight the need to extend protections not only to candidates but also to individuals whose likeness or identity may be misused to manipulate the electorate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the safeguards for non-candidates who may be the subject of such deepfake content within the election period?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fall-out from such a deepfake incident may similarly influence, sway or confuse the electorate, no more than if it were done onto political candidates.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Victor Hugo wisely wrote in Les Miserables, "Whether true or false, what is said about men often has as much influence on their lives and particularly on their destinies as what they do".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Bill aims to deal with the hazards posed by manipulated content during an election.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is now possible, with the assistance of technology, to recreate not only images, but also videos of people, to have them say or appear to do things they never did.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thanks to machine learning, even voice, mouth movements and speaking style can be replicated to create videos that appear authentic.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The video the Minister played in her introductory speech of an AI-generated deepfake video of herself is a chilling example of the power of this technology.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, the example she had shared of President Joe Biden's voice being imitated in robocalls to tell potential Democrat voters not to vote is a recent real-world example of such technology being used in a campaign.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is clear that such technology cannot be left unchecked.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would like the Minister to clarify the intended scope of the word "publish" and whether it is intended to capture, for example, every person that recirculates such a video on social media.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is each share on Facebook, for example, a fresh publication?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If so, I think this should be made clear so that people are mindful about what they share, knowing that they may be taken to have published material if they reshare the video on their own platforms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The law of defamation already treats a person who shares a Facebook post as a potential publisher of that content and I think taking a consistent approach with this is fair.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A related matter is whether Facebook page administrators will be held liable for content posted in the comments of their Facebook pages as publishers of that content.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the UK, courts have held that administrators of Facebook pages can be considered publishers in relation to comments posted by third parties on their page.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And if the intention in this Bill is to extend this duty to Facebook page administrators, it will be good to clarify this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is principled to do so because Facebook page administrators should take responsibility for contents on their page.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In terms of scope, I note that one of the requirements of limb "c" of the operative provisions is that the content must relate to "election in the electoral division".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister can clarify that this is not intended to restrict the implementation, only where it can be shown that the video was related to a particular electoral division.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A video that, for example, falsely attributes criminal or immoral behaviour to a candidate can damage that candidate, even if no reference is made to the constituency the candidate is in, or that such a video is directly related to the election.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would also be grateful if the Minister could clarify the intended scope of the defence in subsection 4 of both proposed amendments that state that the offence in subsection 1 does not apply in any communication between two or more individuals that is private in nature.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But for private communications, is this exception intended to cover any sharing of such messages by private means, such as WhatsApp?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If so, I am concerned this exception may be too broad as, anecdotally, there is already a lot of fake news being circulated through WhatsApp, often forwarded by individuals to others in their group or contacts list.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These may all be known contacts, but if a person forwards a video to several hundred people on his contact list, that may be more damaging than the same video on a Facebook account, precisely because the message comes from a trusted source in a private message channel.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think there is scope to say that if a person forwards a message to, say, a hundred contacts, that would be publication.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, if this exception is to apply to any communications as long as it goes through a private channel, that means these manipulated videos may continue to be circulated through these means and some of the intended mischief may not be captured.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also believe there is scope for legislation to go further in eradicating this threat of manipulated content.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some suggestions for future consideration include, first, this Bill only protects election candidates and only covers them from the time they are indicated as such.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think there would be some scope for extending protection to existing Members of the House and the President as well, since a video circulated ahead of the person being named a candidate in the next election may still do significant damage and there is no reason such harm should not attract punishment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is also a much faster and less burdensome remedy than requiring the person to commence defamation action against any and all those who may have shared a link to such content.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, the offence is currently targeted at a "person", which suggests a natural person.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I will refer to this as deepfakes in the following parts of my speech.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the advent of technology and ubiquity of social media, consumption of digital content is a constant in our daily lives, arguably even a necessity.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are many ways we consume digital content.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are those we search by ourselves in order to keep abreast of current affairs or due to personal interests.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Then, there are some that are shared with us by families and friends.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We often also come across digital content as a result of targeted advertisement algorithms.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is, therefore, safe to presume that all of us would have at some point seen deepfakes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The question is, have we been able to spot them?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And of the digital content that we have viewed and remember, are there any falsities that are wrongly and inadvertently being perpetuated as truths by our memory?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The opening line of the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore's advisory published on 21 March this year accurately addresses the issue.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I quote, "Artificial Intelligence or AI is being used to produce increasingly convincing deepfakes that are indistinguishable or even to the trained eyes".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The question of "whether we will be targeted" is a foregone conclusion.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With our next General Election to be called by November next year, this Bill is a timely defence apparatus against the ever-evolving weaponised deepfakes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Bill will provide a key line of defence against attacks that would invariably seek to strike at the foundation of our democracy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the obvious danger posed by deepfakes would be misleading its audience into believing falsities, viewers could also be confused to the point where one is unable to tell fact from fiction.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The public's awareness of deepfakes, which is what we trying to achieve by a whole-of-society effort, could even be manipulated by bad actors for nefarious purposes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They could, for example, when confronted with matters of record and which are true but adverse to their interests, seek to avoid accountability by falsely claiming that they have been victims of targeted deepfake campaigns.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A phenomenon coined by legal scholars Robert Chesney and Danielle Keats Citron as the "Liar's Dividend".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Clearly, Mr Speaker, we anticipate that we will soon be confronted with novel and previously unimaginable difficulties presented by deepfakes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are gearing up for a battle against deepfakes, not fully knowing who our adversaries are and what their strategies will be.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding, we have to do our best to be ready and ably protect the sanctimony of our democracy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To this end, I raise the following clarifications.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will the Returning Officer be supported in his or her new responsibilities, which are in addition to his or her already existing heavy and critical duties?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thirdly, how will this Bill be operationalised to augment and supplement our current measures against foreign actors and actors who reside outside Singapore, who seek to interfere in our electoral process using deepfakes?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fourthly, section 61MA(4)(a) excludes any communication of content between two or more individuals that is of a private or domestic nature by electronic means.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While this rightly protects freedom of speech and privacy, how can we ensure that the objects of this Bill will not be undermined by the "dark social" phenomenon?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly, while corrective directions may be issued under this Bill, there remains a possibility that it may not reach all of us timeously, or at all.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would the Ministry then consider setting up a digital portal containing a repository of corrections and directions issued under this Bill?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, elections must be fair and just.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When voting, what the voters ought to consider should be the information which the candidates has presented genuinely, not those information which are fabricated or distorted.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, with the advancement of media technology, especially AI, we find that many deceptively realistic videos have spread on social media platforms.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Readers who do not verify with various reliable news sources can easily be misled.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I support this Amendment Bill to ensure that the publication of digitally fabricated and distorted content about the candidates' words and actions will be prohibited during elections.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Here, I would like to pose a few questions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One type of communication not prohibited is messages conveyed privately in family group chats.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask if the Government has considered that this could be exploited as a channel to disseminate fabricated false content during election periods.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed changes will help to ensure that our elections will be conducted in a fair and transparent manner.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to ask the Minister why do the new measures only apply to digitally generated or manipulated content depicting political candidates?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider expanding the scope of content to include indirect representations and depictions?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Candidates in an election would be the most vulnerable to direct and malicious acts of misinformation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, they are just as susceptible to indirect attacks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perpetrators can be creative with their methods and try to find ways around existing legislation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, they could exploit ways to cast doubt on or misrepresent a candidate and what the candidate stands for, without mentioning or depicting the candidates themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would such a potential scenario be covered by any of the existing or proposed pieces of legislation?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other jurisdictions have similar laws in place, including South Korea.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider doing the same as well?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Besides social media platforms, which are under the purview of this Act, we should also consider closing the gap in terms of messaging apps.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Messaging apps, such as WhatsApp and Telegram, are widely used by Singaporeans as key sources of information and news.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I understand the Ministry's intention to maintain the balance between the freedom of expression in private and potential misrepresentation of what a candidate did or said, this is a loophole which may be exploited.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Those with ill intent may exploit this gap in order to ensure that their fake content reaches the widest audiences possible to impact the electoral results.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Besides the social media platforms which are under the purview of this Act, we should also consider closing the gaps in terms of messaging apps.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Messaging apps, such as WhatsApp and Telegram, are widely used by Singaporeans as key sources of information and news.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I understand the Ministry's intention to maintain the balance between the freedom of expression in private and potential misrepresentation of what a candidate did or said, this is a loophole which may be exploited.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill will allow candidates to make a request to the Returning Officer to review content that may breach the prohibition and issue corrective directions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Candidates who have been misrepresented by such content can, in return, make a declaration to attest to the veracity of his/her claim.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: New AI content can be generated very quickly with little expense.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must remain vigilant and be prepared to counter and deal with perpetrators severely, to neutralise their attacks and serve as a deterrent effect.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to effective legislation and enforcement, I urge the Ministry to invest in preventive measures as well, such as identifying, training and empowering new talents in this field in our Ministries and agencies, and adopting advanced technological tools to combat misinformation in elections.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is timely and necessary in an era when technology rapidly transforms how we live, engage with and consume information.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our democracy thrives on citizens' informed choices, which can only be made when voters access accurate, reliable information.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In recent years, we have witnessed how digital platforms have become powerful tools for political engagement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These platforms are integral to modern elections, from campaign advertisements to social media debates.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Voters must cast ballots based on truth, not illusions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But like any powerful tool, it can be misused.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill specifically addresses the risk posed by AI-generated deepfakes, audio or visual content that can make it appear that a candidate said or did something they never did.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Imagine the harm caused by a manipulated video showing a candidate making a statement they never uttered, such as endorsing a controversial policy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If not swiftly addressed, such a video could spread like wildfire across social media, reaching thousands within minutes and distorting public perception before the truth has a chance to catch up.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In the digital world, the truth often struggles to keep pace with lies and by the time the damage is corrected, the harm is usually irreversible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In 2020, a manipulated video of then-Belgian Prime Minister Sophie Wilmès, falsely depicted her blaming environmental damage for the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Although the video was quickly debunked, it spread widely online, illustrating how rapidly deepfakes can mislead the public before the truth emerges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such incidents highlight the urgent need to protect our elections.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As with any legislation that governs speech and expression, there is always the concern that it could be perceived as going too far.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We do not want this Bill to be perceived as inadvertently stifling legitimate debates.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I am pleased that the Bill exempts private communications and news reporting by authorised agencies.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am also glad that candidates have the right to defend themselves against false content.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, we must also be mindful of the potential for abuse.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The corrective request system should not be exploited.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, robust mechanisms must be in place to ensure that only genuine, harmful misinformation is targeted and frivolous complaints are filtered out.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, there is the issue of determining what qualifies as a "realistic enough" representation to be considered misleading.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The subjective nature of this standard could lead to difficulties in enforcement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could the Ministry provide consistent and fair enforcement guidelines?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also worth noting that some of the most concerning platforms, such as WhatsApp and Telegram, operate through private, encrypted messaging systems.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, in Telegram, they do not even have to share their numbers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These platforms allow information to spread rapidly through group chats, yet they remain largely outside the scope of regulatory control due to their private nature.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At this juncture, we need to clarify that it is okay to chat and discuss about politics but wrong to spread deepfakes and misinformation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How can we effectively curtail the spread of misinformation on platforms where content is shielded by encryption?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Should these platforms bear the same responsibility as public social media platforms?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such an initiative could empower Singaporeans to take an active role in reporting misinformation, especially on platforms that are difficult to monitor.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By creating a similar content verification channel, we could involve the public more directly in efforts to counter disinformation, ensuring quicker identification and resolution of misleading content circulating on encrypted platforms.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, I would like to ask how the Government plans to manage the volume of manipulated online content that could be generated during election periods?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will there be dedicated resources or teams to monitor and enforce these regulations in real time and on time?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Given that technology moves very rapidly, how are the tools used updated accordingly?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These platforms are not just passive conduits of information.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are potent actors in shaping public opinion.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Platforms vary significantly in size and influence, some wielding far more power than others.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Should they all be held to the same standard or should penalties scale according to their reach?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What happens if a platform takes too long to respond?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What qualifies as "long enough" in this context?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These are questions we must carefully consider as we strive for effective and fair enforcement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It addresses the growing threat of digitally-manipulated content, reinforces accountability for candidates and platforms and ensures that our democracy remains a place of truth and informed choice.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we look to the future, let us continue to adapt and evolve our laws to meet the challenges of the digital age.
