speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What seems like science fiction today could be a reality in the next election.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points for clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the candidates who have the right to request that corrective directions be issued.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The wordings of the provisions are broad enough to include both situations where the deepfakes prejudice and advantage candidate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, MDDI's public statements appear to suggest that only candidates who have been prejudiced by deepfakes can request corrective directions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, in a press release on 9 September 2024, MDDI stated, "Candidates who have been misrepresented by such content can make a declaration to attest to the veracity of his/her claim." In another media article, a MDDI spokesperson was quoted as saying, "In the case of deepfakes featuring political candidates, we do need the individual to come forward and say that this is a misrepresentation." What if, conversely, the deepfake is beneficial to its subject?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Do other candidates running in the same election have the right to request corrective directions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: AI was used by the main presidential candidates in Argentina's elections in 2023.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to damaging images of the opposing candidate, the candidates also produced favourable deepfake posters of themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Pakistan's 2024 elections, former-Prime Minister Imran Khan's party used AI to create and disseminate speeches based on notes that he passed to his lawyers from prison.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Khan even delivered an AI-generated victory speech after wins by independent candidates backed by his party.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The deepfake may be made of individuals who are not even alive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the Indian state of Tamil Nadu, a political party used AI to recreate video speeches by a long-deceased party leader, in which he complimented current party leaders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A candidate who is benefiting from a deepfake may have no incentive to curb the spread of that deepfake.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point relates to the level of belief necessary to establish the offence of publishing manipulated OEA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the Returning Officer and the Court should determine whether this standard of realism is met?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The timeframe for a Returning Officer to make a corrective direction is much shorter than Court proceedings prosecuting the offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will be more difficult for a requesting candidate to gather evidence within a short timeframe than a prosecution collecting evidence after the fact.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What kind of evidence must the candidate requesting for corrective directions submit?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the requesting candidate or prosecution need to establish actual belief or is potential belief sufficient?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify how the threshold of "some members of the general public" compare to thresholds under other laws which deal with misinformation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, under the tort of defamation, a statement that is defamatory "tends to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under POFMA, a statement of fact is "a statement which a reasonable person seeing, hearing or otherwise perceiving it would consider to be a representation of fact".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, the offence of publishing manipulated OEA only requires the candidate to show that the deepfake would be regarded as genuine by "some members of the general public".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Certain segments of the general public, such as the elderly, are less technologically-savvy and they may regard a deepfake to be genuine more readily than other segments of society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may lead to a situation where material that is found to be manipulated OEA, may not necessarily meet the threshold for the offence of communicating fake statements or facts under POFMA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A candidate may succeed in obtaining a correction directive for manipulated OEA but may not succeed under the tort of defamation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister explain how the level of belief necessary to establish the offence of publishing manipulated OEA compares to the requisite state of mind under other laws which deal with misinformation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the differences in thresholds are intended, can the Minister share the rationale for the differentiated thresholds?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on the exceptions to the ban on deepfakes during elections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As other Members have shared, certain social media or messaging platforms can be used to communicate content to a large number of people, even within private chat groups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: WhatsApp allows for groups of up to 1,024 members; Telegram supports groups of up to 200,000 members; and a person can add up to 5,000 friends on Facebook.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will a message sent to a private group chat with the maximum number of members or a Facebook post, which is set to private but viewable by 5,000 friends, still be considered a private communication?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, Members had expressed concerns about deepfakes even before the debate on this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have heard questions in this House about how we can better tackle impersonation scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Earlier this year, Members Dr Tan Wu Meng and Ms Mariam Jaafar shared concerns about the impact of deepfakes on democratic processes and elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Taken together with today's debate, there is clear consensus on the pressing need to deal with the threat of digitally-manipulated online content because of what is at stake – the integrity of our elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members have also sought clarifications on several issues.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will try my best to address them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some Members have asked how the ELIONA Bill compares to other governments' attempts to tackle deepfakes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have, therefore, scoped the law to be appropriate for Singapore's context.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Earlier, I mentioned how South Korea bans all political campaign videos that used AI-generated content 90 days prior to an election.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is nothing inherently wrong if AI is used, for example, to enhance the background of political communications materials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The key problem is with digitally generated and manipulated content that misrepresents a candidate’s words or actions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members have also asked for the rationale behind the proposed duration of the ban.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Previously, Ms He Ting Ru asked about the recourse for political candidates affected by deepfakes during cooling-off or Polling Day in elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we know that purveyors of deepfakes will not constrain themselves to just the Cooling Off Day or Polling Day.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we are to effectively uphold the integrity of elections, the protections under the Bill must be available when election activities are the most intense and mischief makers most active.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is usually the election period, which is also defined in section 61S of the Parliamentary Elections Act and section 42R of the Presidential Elections Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It starts from the issuance of the Writ of Election and ends after the close of Polling.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms He suggested that the proposed duration of the ban should be longer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This allows for calibration of the speed of response and the resource requirements outside of election periods.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Vikram Nair have asked why the ban was not scoped wider to cover OEA that misrepresents persons other than candidates.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, deepfakes that falsely show key influencers or artistes endorsing a candidate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The question is how influential must these other persons be for the prohibition to apply?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where do we draw the line and who decides?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the political contest develops, the dynamics may also change.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: How about persons who were previously not influential but suddenly gained prominence?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similarly, Ms Pereira asked why the new measures only apply to content that explicitly depicts candidates and not content that indirectly misrepresents them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One such example is an AI-generated podcast that discusses their past.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This problem has existed even without AI or digital manipulation, for example, through coffee shop talk of people who claim to know something about the candidate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the difference is that deepfake content can be very realistic and, hence, persuasive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When they directly depict candidates doing or saying something, the audience is more likely to accept it as reality.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In contrast, hearsay information or third-party accounts like coffee shop chatter tend to be discounted, or at least viewed with some scepticism.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are also practical difficulties in extending the coverage of the ELIONA Bill outside of content directly depicting candidates' words and actions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, how do we ascertain the degree of misrepresentation and whether it warrants prohibition?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The better alternative is to encourage a culture of truthfulness, where persons of influence and candidates themselves step forward to clarify to the public if they have been misrepresented through deepfake content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Voters, too, must be vigilant and turn to trusted sources, such as our mainstream media.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Furthermore, traditional media editing software are now beginning to adopt AI technologies, such as Photoshop's introduction of GenAI capabilities to add and remove content, with photorealistic results.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For instance, if one manually wrote a speech, but uses AI-generation to produce a video of a candidate reading it, the video will be considered to be AI-manipulated and will be prohibited.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This addresses the point raised by Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Vikram Nair also asked if the Bill covers content about a candidate that does not directly relate to the constituency which the candidate is contesting in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A piece of content does not have to refer to the specific constituency which a candidate is contesting in for it to be considered OEA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will make a holistic assessment of what constitutes OEA, and if the online content that misrepresents a candidate has the potential to unduly influence the behaviour of voters in the election.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members, including Mr Louis Ng, Mr Yip and Mr Zhulkarnain, have asked how we will treat OEA designed to entertain, such as satire or memes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, content that does not mislead and deceive people about a candidate’s actual speech or actions will not be banned.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides the question of whether it is digitally generated or manipulated, the law requires us to consider these questions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the public saw or heard the content, would they believe it is the candidate being depicted in the content?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Would they also believe that the candidate did or said that thing in real life?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Memes and satire are already part of our online space.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most of such content will show caricatures of individuals, and a reasonable person will be able to distinguish fact from fiction.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This also applies to other online content, like online political campaign posters.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked what our approach will be if the offending content was labelled, in other words, declared to have been digitally generated or manipulated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A label may not be noticed by everyone.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are also ways to remove labels from content before recirculation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some Members asked for confirmation if the proposed ban covers private or domestic communications, such as messages on WhatsApp and Telegram.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The election rules are not intended to police private or domestic communications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When deciding whether a communication is of a private or domestic nature, the Returning Officer will consider various factors, such as the number of individuals in Singapore who can access the content, if the group is public or closed and the relationships between the individuals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If prohibited content is circulated in these open groups, the Returning Officer will assess if action should be taken.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the same prohibited content is posted online, on websites or social media platforms, we can issue corrective directions for it under the ELIONA Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members, such as Mr Louis Ng and Dr Wan Rizal, asked how we will assess if a piece of content is realistic enough to be believed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But there are some factors that can be considered and I had outlined them in my opening speech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The aim of the ELIONA Bill is to uphold the integrity of our elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have seen how disinformation, even if believed by a small segment of society, can lead to drastic and violent consequences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Consider how allegations of election fraud in the US played a role in the deadly Capitol Hill insurrection on 6 January 2021.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I hope Members will agree that we should not accept any segment, no matter how small, voting based on a false representation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have no way of knowing in advance the extent to which it will alter the course of our elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms He opposed the proposal to allow mainstream media platforms to reproduce content prohibited under the ELIONA Bill when reporting on news and current affairs during the election period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am slightly puzzled because in her speech Ms He also advocated educating the public through short-form videos, which will likely have to reproduce such content in some form to show how realistic they are.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our belief is that news agencies can and should play a part in preserving the integrity of our elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The prohibition does not apply to news published by authorised news agencies because of their duty to report on news fairly and accurately to inform and educate the public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, media outlets report on online scams to educate the public about its dangers and to let citizens know how to identify and avoid scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This often includes republishing images of online content to alert citizens to the scam.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip and other Members sought assurances that the issuance of corrective directions will be impartial and that measures will apply equally, regardless of the party the depicted candidate belongs to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We apply the same criteria to determine who are considered candidates.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are all provided with the choice of when to inform the public of their candidacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The defined election period is also known to all candidates at the same time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The duration and thresholds for content prohibitions are the same for all candidates.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We do not even assess whether the prohibited content is favourable or unfavourable to a candidate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This would be highly subjective and open to dispute.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Deceptive content will not be allowed, whichever party the candidate belongs to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To ensure transparency and accountability, the public will be notified about corrective directions that have been issued against offending content, so that they can vote in an informed manner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Ms Hany Soh's question on how this will be done, ELD will make an assessment and provide an update in due course.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members including Mr Zhulkarnain and Ms He have also asked – what recourse is there if a piece of content was deemed to be wrongfully taken down?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the Returning Officer does not accept their appeal, they may apply to the Courts for judicial review of the Returning Officer's decision.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the content does not otherwise meet the criteria for prohibition, it can be reposted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Ms He's query, there are also current penalties in place for persons other than candidates who knowingly provide false information to Government agencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During this debate and on previous occasions, Members including Ms Sylvia Lim and Ms He have acknowledged the difficulties in determining the authenticity of online media content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why candidates will have to make a declaration in addition to their request to Returning Officer to assess content under the ELIONA Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members will agree that we cannot just take a candidate's word at face value.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Soh highlighted what has been described as "liar's dividend".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why, in addition to the candidate's declaration to the Returning Officer, there is an independent technical assessment made by the Returning Officer and his team of public officers and we have instituted severe penalties for a false declaration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To the question by Mr Louis Ng, candidates will be asked to submit their declarations via an online form during the election period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This form will be available on ELD's candidate services portal.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More details on the information requirements will be shared in due course.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Each of the requests and declarations made by candidates to the Returning Officer will be carefully assessed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Returning Officer will only issue corrective directions for genuine cases that have met the requirements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked if a candidate should instead affirm a statutory declaration for this purpose.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: My colleagues and I have studied the options and weighed the trade-offs between the formal process of making a statutory declaration in front of a Commissioner of Oaths and submitting a declaration online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An online declaration is both efficient and effective.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The offence is an election offence and should be punished in accordance with elections legislation, which provides for the loss of seat for egregious offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The general punishment of making false statutory declarations does not capture the seriousness and context of this offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The digital mode of the declaration is also meant to facilitate a speedy and efficient declaration process for candidates during the election period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the spirit of promoting fair elections, we want to encourage candidates to report content that misrepresents them by removing as many administrative barriers as possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members like Mr Ng have also asked if any candidate can request corrective directions to be issued, not just candidates who are depicted in the impugned content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, we will place significant weight on a depicted candidate's declaration to the Returning Officer as he or she is in the best position to clarify if the content is an accurate representation of himself or herself.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, in most cases, we will rely on candidates making requests and declarations when they are depicted in the impugned content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Further details of the prescribed modality will be shared in future.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In cases of positive campaigning, where the impugned content actually portrays a candidate favourably, other candidates and even non-candidates can make a request for review.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, we will still ask the depicted candidate for a declaration as the Returning Officer and his team are unlikely to have the full facts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the depicted candidate does not make a declaration for whatever reasons, the Government is still empowered to issue directions if we have other objective information that the content is in breach and should be prohibited.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members including Mr Yip and Ms Soh have asked about the timely issuance of corrective directions and safeguards against foreign-based entities who attempt to influence our elections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We recognise the need to quickly disable such false online content about candidates, but there is also the need to be rigorous and fair.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Returning Officer will have to strike a balance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is to minimise the potential harm that such content could cause during our election period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, we already have rules prohibiting foreigners or foreign entities from knowingly publishing or publicly displaying any election advertising.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is in line with the principle that Singapore's politics are for Singaporeans alone to decide.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we are aware of hostile information campaigns or foreign interference, we will address them under the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act, or FICA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms He asked if the penalties for non-compliance by the social media services are too low to have sufficient impact or deterrence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked if the penalties should be scaled according to the platform's reach and impact.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Beyond the exact quantum involved, the imposition of financial penalties on the services for not doing enough to preserve free and fair elections would have reputational implications for the respective platforms, whether from the perspective of Singapore users or globally.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some Members including Ms Pereira asked about tools that the Government will use to detect deepfakes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Deepfake technology is constantly improving and our capabilities must evolve accordingly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I seek Members' understanding that we will err on the side of caution and not reveal the full extent and capabilities of our detection tools.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is to guard against malicious actors who may seek to exploit this information and use it to game or circumvent our systems.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some Members like Dr Wan Rizal and Ms He have asked if the Returning Officer or election officials can proactively monitor the Internet to identify prohibited content and how they will be supported in enforcing provisions under the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During the election, there are processes in place to monitor for and minimise the risk of election interference that can arise from the spread of prohibited OEA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There will be dedicated teams stood up during the election period for this purpose and they will work closely with the social media services to act swiftly on prohibited content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As candidates will be best placed to determine if there is false OEA being circulated, we will rely primarily on their requests to review problematic content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the Returning Officer may still assess and act on problematic content without a candidate's request and declaration if the content is surfaced and deemed likely to threaten electoral integrity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Bill focuses on a specific category of deepfakes during elections while other legislation such as POFMA, OCHA and the Broadcasting Act may be used to tackle other forms of harmful deepfakes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, beyond outrightly harmful consequences, the proliferation of deepfake content is also concerning.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When users can no longer differentiate what is real and what is fake, there is a wider threat to trust in online media.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will mean requiring social media companies to play a larger role in the complex issue of tackling deepfakes, given their extensive influence in shaping our online experiences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MDDI and the IMDA are in the process of engaging the major social media services in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip, Ms He and Ms Soh have asked about our public education efforts to alert our citizens to the dangers of AI-generated misinformation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We agree that a digitally-aware public is the strongest defence we have against misleading and deceptive manipulated online content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Public education plays a critical role in empowering Singaporeans to safeguard themselves against risks in the digital space and be resilient to such threats.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To this end, the Government has put in place public education programmes to equip the public to be discerning producers and consumers of information and protect themselves against online falsehoods.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the National Library's S.U.R.E. programme, which stands for source, understand, research and evaluate, has developed resources and organised activities to educate Singaporeans about the dangers of misinformation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, the National Library Board is currently rolling out its community outreach initiative, Be S.U.R.E.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Together: Gen AI and Deepfakes Edition, which provides opportunities for the public to learn about the uses and threats of generative AI.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We introduced this Bill after careful study of global trends and a realistic assessment of what could happen in Singapore's elections if this threat was left unchecked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I urge all Members to support this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Together, we can ensure that deepfakes and other digitally generated and manipulated content do not prejudice the fair and free elections that Singaporeans should be able to experience.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I just have one clarification on the confusion that the Minister mentioned about my concerns raised about exemption for authorised new agencies and her linking it to one of the suggestions that I made in relation to public education efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: In fact, I think I mentioned in my speech when I talked about the use of pre-bunking in a sort of inoculative approach, I talked about exposing people to weakened forms of misinformation, so, not necessarily real deepfakes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Also, I think when I talked about using short-form content, I was actually referring to generic short-form videos, for example, but not during the election period.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, does not this AI still present the candidate communicating the message as they intended?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Will it be prohibited if it does not misrepresent a candidate's words or actions?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It could be argued that a television image is also a virtual image and is not a real person yet, no one is suggesting that that should be prohibited.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: To cite a real example, would the AI-generated video that the Minister played at the start of her speech be prohibited during elections?
